**Problem fit:** Both proposals address the same core issue (reducing temperature excursions in refrigerated vans) and work within the same constraints (25 delivery runs, 3 staffed shifts, sign-off requirement). Proposal B goes slightly further by explicitly stating how the description of the problem helps put the proposed work in context, showing clearer alignment between problem and solution.

**Feasibility:** Both proposals use the same core method—temperature loggers, driver alerts, and on-duty team checks. However, Proposal B is more feasible: it uses only 2 shifts for checks (22 checks, within the 11-per-shift limit) and converts the third shift into a review meeting, whereas Proposal A attempts to fit all 25 checks into 3 shifts (exceeding capacity at 11 per shift). Proposal B also adds tracking over 6 weeks with comparison to baseline, which is a realistic, measurable timeline.

**Evidence:** Proposal B is significantly stronger here. It specifies weekly tracking for 6 weeks, comparison with the preceding 6 weeks, publication of sample size, and presentation of week-by-week trends. Proposal A only mentions comparing excursion minutes with pre-pilot baseline but lacks detail on frequency, duration, or how results will be communicated.

**Trade-offs:** Neither proposal explicitly discusses material risks or alternatives. Proposal B implicitly handles the trade-off of shift utilization by repurposing the third shift for review, while Proposal A appears to overload the checking capacity. Proposal B’s method of using 2 shifts for checks and 1 for review is a more balanced trade-off.
